page_hint: Ch 18 §18.7 'What We Still Don't Know', third bullet
quoted_clause: **Cross-model distillation opportunities.** Can a 70B 4-bit model be distilled from a 70B FP16 teacher without quality loss, effectively lowering the cost floor? Empirical work needed.
observed: The bullet conflates two different mechanisms. Quantization reduces bit-width of an existing model; distillation trains a new, usually smaller, student model. 'A 70B 4-bit model distilled from a 70B FP16 teacher' is not a well-formed distillation setup - the student would be a different (smaller) model, and the 4-bit part is a separate, already-solved question. The cost-floor claim is also misattributed: quantization already lowers the per-token cost floor (the chapter's own table shows $2.50 -> $0.15/1M), so distillation's contribution is a further reduction in parameter count, not in bit-width.
correction: Rewrite as two distinct questions: (a) does a smaller student distilled from a 70B FP16 teacher reach the quality bar that currently forces requests to the FP16 tier, and what is its serving cost per token; (b) separately, what quality is lost by quantizing the distilled student. Keep the quantization question out of the distillation bullet.
evidence: §18.3.2 already prices the 4-bit tier at $0.15/1M, i.e. the bit-width cost floor is already reflected in the chapter's economics.

page_hint: Ch 18 §18.1 'Concept' bullet list vs §18.3.2 cost table
quoted_clause: **MoE sparse** (selective activation, higher throughput per GPU)

The mechanism is also left out: a 2-of-16 MoE reduces per-token FLOPs but not the weight footprint, so its per-token latency is still dominated by streaming the resident expert weights, and its throughput advantage appears only when batching amortizes that streaming across many sequences. As written, a reader may expect an MoE tier to be both cheaper and faster per request.
correction: Qualify the claim: 'MoE sparse (selective activation: fewer FLOPs per token at the same weight footprint; throughput advantage requires batching to amortize weight streaming, and per-request latency can be higher than a dense tier of the same size)'. Add a sentence reconciling it with the 300 ms figure.
evidence: §18.3.2: 70B dense 8-bit = $1.25 / 250 ms; 70B MoE 8-bit = $1.00 / 300 ms. §18.3.1: MoE FP16 = 140 GB, the same as dense FP16.

quoted_clause: Prefix-cache eviction moves neither: the request still carries the full accumulated context (34.0 GB at turn 4), so its own KV is unchanged — what changes is the reusable cached prefix, which is freed and must be re-prefilled on the next turn.

page_hint: Ch 19 §8 'Conditional completed-agent percentiles' vs. 'Unconditional fallback-inclusive ledger'
quoted_clause: the *incremental* agent work beyond the single-shot baseline is zero, so it adds nothing to the p90/p95 values

correction: State all three conventions explicitly: (i) conditional on completed runs (98% renormalized): p50/p90/p95 = 220/440/660 ms; (ii) unconditional with the fallback zero-weighted: p95 = 440 ms (the 2% mass sorts to the bottom); (iii) unconditional with the fallback at its true 860 ms: p95 = 660 ms, p99 = 860 ms.
evidence: Under the zero-turn convention the fallback contributes 0 ms of added orchestration, so it sorts to the *bottom* of the unconditional distribution: CDF(≤220 ms) = 2% + 68% = 70%; CDF(≤440 ms) = 95.0%; CDF(≤660 ms) = 100%. The unconditional p95 therefore reads 440 ms, not 660 ms. The chapter states this itself: 'under the zero-turn convention it lands exactly on the boundary, CDF(T ≤ 2) = 95.0%, and reads T = 2 → 440 ms'. The p90 is unchanged (440 ms) but the p95 changes from 660 ms to 440 ms.
